## Part 1 — Setup and Cleaning

**Goal:** download your two novels, strip off the Gutenberg header and footer from each, and end up with a clean list of lowercase words for each book.

-   Download both novels (Plain Text UTF-8) into `../../data/gutenberg/` — or wherever your `hw4` folder expects them — with clear filenames.
-   Read each one in with `.readlines()`, inside a `try`/`except` so a bad filename doesn't crash the whole document.

```{python}
import re
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

try:
    with open("../../data/gutenberg/great_gatsby.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        great_gatsby_lines = f.readlines()
    with open("../../data/gutenberg/candide.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        candide_lines = f.readlines()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("Couldn't find a file — check the filename and location.")
```

-   Use your `while` loops to chop the header off the front and the footer off the back of each book, the same way you did with *Alice*.

```{python}
while not great_gatsby_lines[0].startswith("*** START"):
    great_gatsby_lines = great_gatsby_lines[1:]    
great_gatsby_lines = great_gatsby_lines[1:]        

while not great_gatsby_lines[-1].startswith("*** END"):
    great_gatsby_lines = great_gatsby_lines[:-1]    
great_gatsby_lines = great_gatsby_lines[:-1]        

great_gatsby_text = "".join(great_gatsby_lines)

while not candide_lines[0].startswith("*** START"):
    candide_lines = candide_lines[1:]    
candide_lines = candide_lines[1:]       

while not candide_lines[-1].startswith("*** END"):
    candide_lines = candide_lines[:-1]    
candide_lines = candide_lines[:-1]       

candide_text = "".join(candide_lines)
```

-   Glue the lines back together, lowercase, and split into words with `re.split()`, removing any empty strings left behind.

```{python} 
great_gatsby_words = re.split(r"[\W]+", great_gatsby_text.lower())
great_gatsby_words = [w for w in great_gatsby_words if w != ""]

candide_words = re.split(r"[\W]+", candide_text.lower())
candide_words = [w for w in candide_words if w != ""]
```

*I imported re for regular-expressions to maipulate the text files I downloaded from Project Gutenberg, then I imported matplotlib.pyplot for plotting charts later. I used try to open the text files for The Great gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald and Candide by Voltaire for the ../../data/gutenberg/ directory, and readlines() to store each file as a list of lines. I used except to print a file not found error message in case the file could not be found to prevent the program from crashing. I then used while loops to remove the header and footer from each text. I was able to use startswith() to remove lines by list slicing until the the loop reached the lines that contained START and END and then I got rid of those lines. I finally used "".join() to combine the cleaned lines back into a single string for each text. I did not use AI for this section since we went over this code in class. Instead, I only subsituted the alice.txt and mansfield.txt labels with the titles of the two novels and kept the other parts of the code the same. *

## Part 2 — Tokens, Types, and a Fair Comparison

**Goal:** compare the vocabulary richness of your two books, correctly.

-   For each book, report the total word count (tokens), the number of unique words (types), and the type–token ratio. 

*Gatsby tokens: 50,005, Candide tokens: 36,174, Gatsby unique types: 5,840, Candide unique types: 5,122, Gatsby TTR: 0.1168, Candide TTR: 0.1416*

```{python}
print("Gatsby tokens:", len(great_gatsby_words))
print("Candide tokens:", len(candide_words))
print("Gatsby unique types:", len(set(great_gatsby_words)))
print("Candide unique types:", len(set(candide_words)))
```
```{python}
great_gatsby_ttr = len(set(great_gatsby_words)) / len(great_gatsby_words)
candide_ttr = len(set(candide_words)) / len(candide_words)
print("Great Gatsby TTR:", great_gatsby_ttr)
print("Candide TTR:", candide_ttr)
```

-   Compare the two raw TTRs — which book looks like it has the richer vocabulary?

*It appears that Candide has a richer vocabulary than The Great Gatsby since it has a higher TTR.*

-   Now compute the TTR of just the first 10,000 words of each book, and compare again. Explain, in your own words, why this second comparison is the fairer one.

*Candide has a TTR of 0.2368 at the first 10,000 words while The Great Gatsby has a TTR of only 0.2283 at the first 10,000 words. It appears that Candide still has a richer vocabulary than The Great Gatsby since it maintains a higher TTR even when calculated from the first 10,000 words of the text. This comparison is fairer because both texts are being measured using the same number of words, which reduce sthe influence of difference between their total lengths.*

```{python}
great_gatsby_ttr_10000 = len(set(great_gatsby_words[:10000])) / len(great_gatsby_words[:10000])
candide_ttr_10000 = len(set(candide_words[:10000])) / len(candide_words[:10000])
print("Great Gatsby TTR (10,000 words):", great_gatsby_ttr_10000)
print("Candide TTR (10,000 words):", candide_ttr_10000)
```

-   Report the average word length for each book.

*The Great Gatsby has an average word length of 4.13 letters per word, while Candide has an average word length of 4.36 letters per word.*

```{python}
great_gatsby_wd_len_total = 0
for w in great_gatsby_words:
    great_gatsby_wd_len_total += len(w)
great_gatsby_avg_word_len = great_gatsby_wd_len_total / len(great_gatsby_words)

candide_wd_len_total = 0
for w in candide_words:
    candide_wd_len_total += len(w)
candide_avg_word_len = candide_wd_len_total / len(candide_words)

print("Great Gatsby Average Word Length:", great_gatsby_avg_word_len)
print("Candide Average Word Length:", candide_avg_word_len)
``` 

*Explain your code for this part, and disclose any AI use. I used len() i n order to count the total number of words in each novel by measuring the length of the great_gatsby_words and candide_words lists. The counts represent tokens, which means that every appearence of a word is counted, even if it repeats itself. I then used set() to remove duplicate words (to ensure a accurate TTR by preserving distinct words) and then len() to count each unique word in each text. I then divided the number of unique types by the total number of tokens to get the TTR. The higher a TTR, the larger the amount of different words in comparison to the total number of words in a text. I purposely chose two texts I knew were similar in length to get a more intertetsing and accurate comparison. Then I used list slicing to select the first 10,000 words from each text. I used set() and len() to cont the unique word sin the sleection of 10,000 words and then calculated the TTR in the same way before. Even thought the two texts are similar in length anyway using the first 10,000 words made the comparison fair because the selections were equal in size. Candide had a higher TTR than Gatsby but the difference was small. For average word length, I made a variable for the word length of each text at zero, then I used a for loop to go through every or din each word list, and adding len(w) to the total. Finally, I divided the total word length by the number of words to get the average word length. Candide has a higher average, at 4.36 letters per word, while The Great Gatsby has an average word length of 4.13 letters per word. I only used AI when prompted to autofill code I was in the middle of writing which I reocogized was not going to fill my code with code which I did not need. If the autofill was not useful I ignored and wrote the rest myself. I understood list slicing from hw3.*

## Part 4 — Visualize It

**Goal:** show your findings as charts.

-   Make **one bar chart** comparing your two authors on a single measure of your choice from Part 3.
```{python}
books = ["The Great Gatsby - F. Scott Fitzgerald", "Candide - Voltaire"]
ly_rates = [great_gatsby_ly_rate, candide_ly_rate]

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.bar(books, ly_rates)
plt.title("Words Ending In -ly per 1,000 Words")
plt.xlabel("Novel and Author")
plt.ylabel("Rate per 1,000 Words")
plt.savefig("ly_rate_comparison_chart.png")
plt.show()
```
-   Make **one Zipf plot** — rank vs. frequency, log scale on both axes — with **both** books on the same chart, each with its own label and a legend.
-   Every chart needs a title, axis labels, and should be saved to a file with `plt.savefig()`.

```{python}
great_gatsby_freq = Counter(great_gatsby_words)
candide_freq = Counter(candide_words)

great_gatsby_freqs = sorted(great_gatsby_freq.values(), reverse=True)
candide_freqs = sorted(candide_freq.values(), reverse=True)

great_gatsby_ranks = range(1, len(great_gatsby_freqs) + 1)
candide_ranks = range(1, len(candide_freqs) + 1)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.plot(great_gatsby_ranks, great_gatsby_freqs, label="The Great Gatsby")
plt.plot(candide_ranks, candide_freqs, label="Candide")

plt.xscale("log")
plt.yscale("log")
plt.title("Word Frequency By Rank")
plt.xlabel("Word rank (log scale)")
plt.ylabel("Frequency (log scale)")
plt.legend()
plt.savefig("zipf_rank_comparison_chart.png")
plt.show()
```


*I used matplotlib to create the bar chart and Zipf plot to compare each text. For the bar chart, I used the ly rates that I calculated in Part 3 and used the plt.xlabel to label the text title and author and the plt.ylabel to plot the rate per 1000 words. I put the ly rates in a single list to make it easier to pass to the plt.bar function. For the Zipf plot, I used Counter(great_gatsby_words) and Counter(candide_words) to count every time eah word appears in each text. I used .values() to retieve the frequency counts without the word strings. I then used sorted() to order the frequencies form largest to smallest. I used range to create the rank numbers for the horizontal axis. Each plt.plot was used to label the text and plot the frequency of each word by its rank. plt.xscale("log") and plt.yscale("log") were used to set both axes to a log scale. plt.legend() displayed the labels and plt.savefig() saves the chart as an image. I used AI to auto fill the .values() and reverse=True commands as I was unsure of the exact syntax. It also autofilled the figize(10,6)) but other than that the other parts of the code I adapted from previous charting activities with alice.text and mansfield.txt. The log functions I knew to use beforehand based on prior experience using online graphs.*

## Quick Reference

Here is a quick reference for the Python techniques you will need to use in this assignment. You can copy and paste these snippets into your own code, but make sure you understand what each one does before you do.

| What you need to do | How |
|---|---|
| Read a file line by line | `with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f: lines = f.readlines()` |
| Handle a bad filename without crashing | `try: ... except FileNotFoundError: ...` |
| Chop lines off the front while a condition holds | `while not lines[0].startswith("..."): lines = lines[1:]` |
| Chop lines off the back while a condition holds | `while not lines[-1].startswith("..."): lines = lines[:-1]` |
| Glue a list of lines back into one string | `"".join(lines)` |
| Split text into words, removing punctuation | `re.split(r"[\W]+", text.lower())`, then drop empty strings |
| Count tokens / types / TTR | `len(words)`, `len(set(words))`, `len(set(words)) / len(words)` |
| Slice the first N items | `words[:10000]` |
| Running total inside a loop | `total = 0` then `total += len(w)` for each `w` |
| Turn a count into a rate per 1,000 | `count / len(words) * 1000` |
| Check the start/end of a string | `word.startswith("un")`, `word.endswith("ly")` |
| Build a filtered list in one line | `[w for w in words if condition(w)]` |
| Count and rank items | `Counter(words).most_common(n)` |
| Bar chart | `plt.bar(labels, values)` |
| Line chart with a log–log scale | `plt.plot(ranks, freqs)` then `plt.xscale("log")`, `plt.yscale("log")` |
| Multiple lines on one chart with a legend | `plt.plot(x, y, label="...")` for each, then `plt.legend()` |

3.  **Get the folder's GitHub address.** On github.com, navigate into your repo to `homework/hw4`, and copy the URL from your browser's address bar. It'll look like:

    ```
    https://github.com/your-username/LIN_301/tree/main/homework/hw4
    ```

4.  **Submit that link on Canvas** — no file upload needed.
5.  Be sure to replace "lastname_firstname" with your actual last name and first name in your `.qmd` filename.
